fields.Description: A guide introducing readers to eight types of cheese that may appear unusual or intimidating due to their look or smell but are surprisingly delicious and approachable. 8 Cheeses That Taste Better Than You Expect 

 
 

 
 

 
 
 
 

 
 


 

 

April 24, 2026 

 

 

 


Ian Zygmunt 



 

 
 
 
We have all been there. You are standing at the cheese counter, staring at a wedge that looks a little too fuzzy, a little too pungent, or just plain weird. You instinctively reach for the safe block of cheddar or the familiar brie. 
 
But here is a secret the experts know: some of the most intimidating cheeses are actually the most delicious, approachable, and crowd-pleasing options in the case. 
 
If you are ready to trade “safe” for “spectacular,” this guide is for you. Here are eight cheeses that look or smell challenging but deliver flavors you will fall in love with immediately. 
 

1. Taleggio: The “Bark Is Worse Than Its Bite” Cheese 

 
If you judge Taleggio by its aroma, you might run the other way. This Italian washed-rind cheese is famous for a pungent, yeasty smell often described as “barnyardy.” 
 
However, the smell is entirely in the thin, pinkish-orange rind. Once you cut past that, the pale interior is incredibly mild, buttery, and fruity. It has a texture similar to thick custard and melts on the tongue with a gentle tang that is far less aggressive than its scent suggests. 
 

How to serve it: 
Spread it on crusty sourdough. The yeasty bread complements the cheese perfectly. It is also one of the best melting cheeses for a grown-up grilled cheese sandwich. 
 

2. Brunost (Gjetost): The Cheese That Thinks It’s Fudge 

 
This Norwegian specialty stops people in their tracks because it is brown. Not just on the outside, but all the way through. It looks like a block of caramel, and surprisingly, it tastes like one too. 
 
Brunost is made by boiling whey until the natural sugars caramelize. The result is a dense, sweet, and savory cheese with notes of butterscotch and dulce de leche. It is widely different from the salty, savory profile we expect from cheese, which makes it a delightful surprise for anyone with a sweet tooth. 
 

How to serve it: 
Slice it paper-thin (using a cheese plane is essential here) and serve it on warm waffles or toast. It is effectively a breakfast cheese that pairs beautifully with coffee. 
 

3. Mimolette: The Bright Orange Cannonball 

 
Mimolette looks intimidating. It comes in a cratered, dusty ball that resembles a cantaloupe or a moon rock. The rind is hard and craggy, and the interior is a shocking, vibrant orange. 
 
Despite its rugged exterior, Mimolette is remarkably easy to love. It is essentially the French answer to Edam, but aged until it becomes hard and brittle. The flavor is intensely nutty, with distinct notes of toasted hazelnut and butterscotch. It lacks the sharp “bite” of an aged cheddar, offering a smoother, sweeter finish that is very snackable. 
 

How to serve it: 
You cannot slice this cheese easily; you have to shard it. Use a sharp knife to chip off nuggets and serve them alongside dark chocolate or dried apricots. 
 

4. Gorgonzola Dolce: The “Blue” for People Who Hate Blue 

 
Blue cheese is the most common phobia at the cheese counter. The metallic, spicy sting of mold can be overwhelming. But not all blues are built the same. 
 
“Dolce” literally means sweet. This version of Gorgonzola is younger and creamier than its firmer, spicier cousins (often labeled “Piccante”). It is so soft it is often spoonable. The blue veins are present, but the flavor is milky, creamy, and gentle, lacking the aggressive ammonia bite that scares people away from blue cheese. It is practically savory ice cream. 
 

How to serve it: 
Don’t crumble it; scoop it. Drop a dollop onto a slice of pear or drizzle it with honey. It also melts beautifully into warm polenta. 
 

5. Halloumi: The Squeaky Grilling Cheese 

 
Halloumi can be confusing if you try to eat it raw. It is rubbery, salty, and has a texture that squeaks against your teeth. It feels wrong. 
 
But Halloumi is not meant to be eaten cold. It is a non-melting cheese, meaning you can throw it directly into a frying pan or onto a grill grate. When heat is applied, the exterior turns crispy and golden brown, while the inside softens into a savory, chewy delight that tastes like a mozzarella stick without the breading. The “squeak” becomes a satisfying chew that makes it a fantastic meat substitute. 
 

How to serve it: 
Slice it into thick slabs and fry it in a dry pan until golden. Squeeze fresh lemon juice over the top to cut the saltiness. 
 

6. Ash-Ripened Goat Cheese: The Gray Layer 

 
You might see a log of goat cheese coated in gray powder, or a beautiful white pyramid with a stark black line running through the center. This is vegetable ash (often made from dried vines or vegetables). 
 
While eating “ash” sounds unappealing, it is flavorless and odorless. It is used by cheesemakers to balance the acidity of the cheese. As a result, ash-ripened goat cheeses are often mellower, sweeter, and less “goaty” than the bright white fresh chèvre you buy in plastic tubs. The texture is often lighter and fluffier, like a cloud. 
 

How to serve it: 
This is the centerpiece of a cheese board. The visual contrast is stunning. Serve it with crisp white wine and green apples. 
 

7. Cottage Cheese: The Comeback Kid 

 
For years, cottage cheese was trapped in the reputation of being a bland, watery diet food from the 1980s. 
 
Modern, high-quality cottage cheese is a different animal. When you buy whole-milk (4% fat) varieties from good producers, the curds are creamy and rich, not watery. It has a mild, milky savoriness similar to fresh burrata or mozzarella. It is a blank canvas high in protein that works just as well with savory toppings as it does with fruit. 
 

How to serve it: 
Treat it like savory dip. Top a bowl with cucumbers, high-quality olive oil, sea salt, and cracked pepper. You will never look at it as “diet food” again. 
 

8. Aged Gouda: The Crunchy Butterscotch Bomb 

 
Most people know Gouda as the red-waxed, rubbery circles in the supermarket dairy aisle. That young cheese is mild and lunchbox-friendly, but forgettable. 
 
Aged Gouda (often labeled as aged 18 months or more) is a transformation. As it loses moisture, it develops a deep amber color and a hard, crystalline texture. Those white crunchy bits you feel? They aren’t salt; they are protein crystals (tyrosine) that form during aging. The flavor becomes profoundly sweet, tasting of salted caramel, whiskey, and pecans. It is more like candy than cheese. 
 

How to serve it: 
Cube it and eat it at room temperature. It needs nothing else, though it pairs exceptionally well with a dark stout beer or bourbon.
